---
title: "Quiz: diffusion models and generated detail"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** In the forward process, what happens to an image as $\tau$ goes from 0 to 1, and what does the noise schedule decide?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Signal $\sqrt{\bar\alpha}$, noise $\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The signal is shrunk and Gaussian noise is added until only noise is left ($\bar\alpha \approx 0$). The schedule decides how fast: how much signal remains at each time.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why is training a denoiser "supervised learning with free labels"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Who added the noise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
We take clean training images and add noise ourselves, so the correct answer (the noise, or the clean image) is known for every training example without any annotation.
:::

---

**Q3.** At very high noise, what does the best possible denoiser output?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the best guess when the noisy image says almost nothing?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The average of all clean images compatible with the noisy one; at the highest noise, the average of the whole training set: a blurry mean image, not a sample.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does sampling with very few steps give blurry or "in-between" results?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Q3.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each step jumps towards the denoiser's estimate, which at high noise is an average of many images. With few steps the sample ends near such an average (between modes); many small steps let the estimate refine at lower noise levels, where it follows one mode.
:::

---

**Q5.** A diffusion model was trained to perfection on 50 images. What will its samples be?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What distribution does a perfect denoiser of 50 images describe?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Copies of the 50 training images: the perfect denoiser of a finite set generates exactly that set. Real networks generate new images because they are imperfect (they smooth between examples).
:::

---

**Q6.** What does a strong guidance weight do to conditional samples?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Typical versus diverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They become more typical of the condition and less diverse: samples move to where the condition is most certain and away from anything that might also fit another condition.
:::

---

**Q7.** A restoration's posterior mean and one posterior sample: which has the higher PSNR on average, and which looks more realistic?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Averaging removes uncertain detail.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The mean has the higher PSNR (it minimises the expected squared error; a sample has twice the error for a Gaussian posterior). The sample looks more realistic: it is sharp everywhere, but its uncertain details come from the prior.
:::

---

**Q8.** A generatively restored image shows two nucleoli in a cell whose nucleoli are smaller than the blur of the raw image. May you report "two nucleoli"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does detail below the resolution come from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Below the resolution of the measurement the detail comes from the prior (the training images). Count on the raw data, or validate the count on images with ground truth, and check whether several samples agree.
:::

---

**Q9.** Why is a prior that has never seen a rare phenotype dangerous for restoration?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the posterior do with something it cannot explain?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It explains the measurement with the closest normal training images, so the rare phenotype is "corrected" to normal. The result looks convincing, and even samples agree on it, so nothing warns you.
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* $x_0 = 3$, $\sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.6$, $\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} = 0.8$, $\varepsilon = 0.5$. Compute $x_\tau$ and its variance given $x_0$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$x_\tau = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}\,\varepsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$x_\tau = 1.8 + 0.4 = 2.2$. Given $x_0$ the variance is $1 - \bar\alpha = 0.64$.
:::
